brief.orientation: For a small course or coaching team collecting student feedback for course and cohort sales pages, Senja is a tool for requesting text or video testimonials and displaying or reusing the responses.
brief.arc: Single email, so the whole arc is inside it: name the ask that never gets sent (the second one), turn it into a documented setting with exact numbers, name the order-of-operations catch that makes the setting worth acting on now, then ask for the free account.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email was requested, so the only real decision is which single argument to spend it on. Four shelves could carry this campaign: product breadth (21 facts, none strong enough to lead), display and reuse (widgets, reels, Wall of Love), commercial terms (price, the 15-testimonial Free limit), and the asking mechanism. The asking mechanism wins because it is the one tied to a verified problem for this exact reader — P1 (does not know how to get them, does not want to seem pushy) and P3 (praise does not become a testimonial unless you ask, and ask promptly) — and because the previous campaign's rework note identified precisely this: the ask that produces the testimonial is usually the second one, and the second ask is a setting rather than a question of nerve. Display and reuse is the better-stocked shelf but answers a question this reader has not reached; pricing is checkable but leads with a cost before a reason. The objection assigned is the one the verified material actually supports — reminders landing on students they have a relationship with — and it has a bounded, documented answer in E27 (three, at 1/3/7 days, only to non-responders). What it does not have, and what the email must not supply, is evidence that students perceive this as non-pushy or that timely asks yield stronger testimonials; both are explicitly unsupported, so the copy argues from the mechanism and the control, never from the reaction. No proof shelf exists at all — no named customer, no quote, no outcome — so the email asks the reader to test rather than believe, which is also why the self-serve signup is the honest destination for the primary bet.

emails.selection_reason: This reader's verified blocker is not the display of testimonials, it is sending the ask — and specifically sending it twice. Senja documents the second and third ask as a bounded setting on the invite (three emails, 1/3/7 days, non-responders only) with a hard prerequisite: it only applies to invites sent after the switch is on. That makes the useful next decision immediate and concrete for someone with a cohort to invite, and it is supported without needing a customer result, a named reference or a claim about how students react.

emails.single_idea: The ask that gets answered is usually the second one, and in Senja the second ask is a setting rather than a decision: switch follow-ups on and up to three reminders go out 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, to the students who have not answered — but only on invites you send after the switch is on, so the order matters.
emails.felt_need: A newly launched course creator reports not knowing how to obtain testimonials and feeling reluctant to ask for reviews because it could seem pushy. Neera reports that praise does not automatically become strong testimonials: asking appropriately and promptly matters, and delayed requests can produce weaker recollections.
emails.mechanism: Follow-ups are a toggle on the invite, not a second email you have to write and decide to send. Turn them on and Senja sends up to three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, and only to students who haven't responded yet. The catch is the whole reason to do this before the next batch goes out: follow-ups only apply to invites sent after you turn them on — students invited before that get no reminders at all. The condition on the payoff is simply having a Senja account and the invite set up there: you verify your email, give your name, website and plan choice, and you can start on Free.
